paras: The threatened lynching of Luther Thompson occurred in late August 1900, when Thompson, a Black tenant farmer jailed at New Decatur, Alabama, on charges of horse stealing and attempted criminal assault on a white woman, was reported in danger of being lynched by the people of Cedar Grove in Morgan County. No attack on him is reported, and the coverage does not show what became of him. A Birmingham paper's special dispatch was condensed by the wire and reprinted in papers from New Jersey to North Dakota, and a Black weekly in Kansas City predicted his death.

According to the Age-Herald of Birmingham, Thompson was a tenant on the plantation of Jackson Thompson near Cedar Grove, about fifteen miles southwest of New Decatur. The paper said that on Monday night he took a quantity of his landlord's clothing and one of his best horses and rode away.

The same account charged that he then hid by the public highway and seized Mrs. Maggie Williams, described as "a highly respectable white woman," as she passed. In the paper's telling, she fought him off and screamed for help, and her attacker fled on the stolen horse. When she reported it the story "created intense excitement," and once the crime was laid to Thompson there was "bold talk of lynching."

Meanwhile Thompson reached Decatur and offered the horse to Wallace Bros., liverymen, who grew suspicious, refused to buy it and notified the police. Police arrested him on Bank street and jailed him, and Jackson Thompson came to the city and identified the horse as his. The New Decatur special of August 29 said he was "in grave danger of lynching at the hands of the people of Cedar Grove."
No later report on Thompson, whether of a lynching, a trial or a release, appears in either press in the following month.

The Age-Herald ran the story on its front page under the headline "Luther Thompson May Stretch Hemp," stated the accusations as fact, and described the alleged attacker as springing on Mrs. Williams "like a beast of prey" and as a "black brute." A condensed version naming Mrs. Williams went out over the wire under headlines such as "A Probable Lynching" in the Louisville Courier-Journal and "May Be Another Lynching" in The Sun. The Rock Island Argus in Illinois headed it "He'll Be Lynched, All Right."

Copies appeared into mid-September in Woodstock, Vt., Abilene, Washburn, N.D., and Middleburgh, Pa., some datelined Birmingham and credited to the Age-Herald. The Americus Times-Recorder in Georgia printed "purse stealing" in place of horse stealing, while weekly digests and a San Antonio column of telegraph brevities reduced the case to a single line.

The only Black-press notice found, in the American Citizen of Kansas City, ran in a column of news briefs on August 31. It predicted that Thompson "will doubtless be lynebed ere many more suns" and dismissed the attempted-rape charge as the "usual 'pretty white girl'" story, a skepticism absent from every white report.

The Age-Herald dispatch said Thompson was "arrested here today," August 29, yet its own narrative has him offering the horse for sale the morning after the Monday-night theft and arrested soon after. Later copies placed the arrest variously at New Decatur, Decatur or Birmingham, but these follow the datelines of relays of the same special.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Luther Thompson
bases: Thompson, jailed on charges of horse stealing and attempted assault on a white woman, was reported in 'grave danger of lynching' amid 'bold talk of lynching' at Cedar Grove; no attack on him is reported (A1, A2, A7).
The coverage reports only a threatened lynching by 'the people of Cedar Grove' over an alleged crime; no killing is reported and no follow-up on Thompson's fate was found (A1, A2, A8).
Every report, including the Black-press brief, repeats or condenses the Age-Herald's New Decatur special, which later copies credit by name (A1, A8, A12, A13).

accounts.label: Age-Herald special from New Decatur
accounts.gist: Thompson stole clothing and a horse Monday night, attacked Mrs. Williams by the roadside, fled, and was arrested after trying to sell the horse; Cedar Grove talked of lynching him.

accounts.label: Wire condensation
accounts.gist: A negro charged with horse stealing and attempted assault on a white woman was arrested and in imminent danger of lynching at Cedar Grove.

accounts.label: Black press brief
accounts.gist: Thompson would 'doubtless be lynebed'; the attempted-rape charge was dismissed with sarcasm as the 'usual' story.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald neither urged nor condemned a lynching but headlined 'Luther Thompson May Stretch Hemp', stated the accusation as fact, and called him 'the brute' and 'darkey'.
Out-of-state papers ran the condensed dispatch under headlines such as 'A Probable Lynching' and, in Rock Island, 'He'll Be Lynched, All Right'.
The American Citizen treated the lynching as near-certain and scoffed at the 'usual "pretty white girl"' charge.

versions.value: Aug. 29 ('today' in the Aug. 29 dispatch; 'yesterday' in Aug. 30-31 datelines)
The morning after the Monday-night theft (Aug. 28), implied by the Age-Herald narrative

conflicts.note: The Age-Herald's own story says he offered the horse for sale 'the next morning' and was arrested 'a short time after', which conflicts with its 'arrested here today'.
The Americus copy's 'purse stealing' is a lone variant of the wire text; the original Age-Herald special says horse.
The Birmingham datelines are relays of the Age-Herald special; the arrest was at New Decatur.

record_check.dossier: The threat was reported in a dispatch dated Aug. 29, 1900; the alleged crimes were on Monday night, Aug. 27.
